title: ffmpeg
description: FFmpeg is a free command-line toolkit for recording, converting, and streaming audio and video.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
This page covers installing FFmpeg and the command structure every
invocation shares, so the examples on later pages make sense at a glance.

## 1. Install FFmpeg

| Platform | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Arch Linux | `sudo pacman -S ffmpeg` |
| Debian / Ubuntu | `sudo apt install ffmpeg` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install ffmpeg` |
| openSUSE | `sudo zypper install ffmpeg` |
| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install ffmpeg` |
| Windows | Download a build from [gyan.dev](https://www.gyan.dev/ffmpeg/builds/) and add it to `PATH` |

Verify it installed correctly, and see which codecs your build supports:

```bash
ffmpeg -version
ffmpeg -codecs   # long list of every encoder/decoder available
```

## 2. Anatomy of an ffmpeg command

Every invocation follows roughly the same shape:

```bash
ffmpeg [global opts] -i input [input opts] [output opts] output
```

A few rules that explain most confusing behavior:

- **Options apply to the file that follows them.** `-i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 out.mp4`
  applies `-c:v libx264` to the *output*, because it comes after the
  output is named — not to the input.
- **Order matters for timing flags.** `-ss` before `-i` seeks quickly by
  jumping to the nearest keyframe; `-ss` after `-i` seeks frame-accurately
  but slower, by decoding from the start.
- **`-c` means codec, `:v`/`:a`/`:s` pick the stream type.** `-c:v` sets
  the video codec, `-c:a` the audio codec, `-c copy` means "copy every
  stream without re-encoding."
- **Multiple inputs and outputs are both allowed.** You can pass several
  `-i` flags and several output files in one invocation; `-map` decides
  which streams from which input go to which output. See
  [Filters & filtergraphs](/ffmpeg/filters/) for the syntax this unlocks.

## 3. Run your first conversion

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.mov output.mp4
```

FFmpeg picks sensible default codecs for the output container unless you
override them with `-c:v`/`-c:a`. Progress prints to stderr as it runs; add
`-hide_banner -loglevel error` to quiet the build/config banner and most
status noise.

## 4. Inspect a file before editing it

```
ffprobe input.mp4
ffprobe -v error -show_format -show_streams input.mp4
```

`ffprobe` ships alongside `ffmpeg` and prints container, codec, resolution,
duration, and bitrate without touching the file. This is the single most
useful habit to build early: run it on any file before assuming what
codec, resolution, or frame rate it actually has, especially files someone
else handed you. Continue to
[Common Operations](/ffmpeg/common-operations/) for transcoding, trimming,
and extracting audio, or jump straight to the
[Command Reference](/ffmpeg/command-reference/) for a cheat sheet.

## Build flavors & codec support

The `ffmpeg` package in most distro repos is built with a
conservative set of codecs to avoid patent-licensing issues. Two common
gaps:

- **libx264/libx265** (H.264/H.265 encoding) — almost always
  included, but confirm with `ffmpeg -encoders | grep 264`.
- **libfdk\_aac** — often excluded for licensing reasons; the
  built-in `aac` encoder is used instead and is good enough for most
  purposes.

On Arch Linux, the official `ffmpeg` package is a "full" build with
essentially everything enabled (libx264, libx265, libvpx, libaom-av1,
libsvtav1, libopus, VAAPI, NVENC support, etc.), so build-flavor gaps
mostly matter on more conservative distros or minimal Docker base images.
If you ever need to check a remote server or container image rather than
your own desktop, this is the first thing worth checking.

```bash
ffmpeg -version                 # shows the full ./configure flags used to build it
ffmpeg -encoders | grep -i 265   # check whether a specific encoder is available
```

## 5. Where to go next

- New to the codec/container distinction? Start with
  [Containers & Codecs](/ffmpeg/containers-codecs/).
- Want the everyday commands (trim, convert, extract audio, resize)?
  See [Common Operations](/ffmpeg/common-operations/).
- Just need to look something up? The
  [Command Reference](/ffmpeg/command-reference/) is a flat cheat sheet.

Core Concepts.Containers & Codecs:
The single most common source of confusion for people new to FFmpeg:
**a file extension is a container, not a codec**. Understanding the
difference explains most of what `-c:v`, `-c:a`, and remuxing
actually do.

## What's the difference?

- A **codec** (coder-decoder) is the algorithm that compresses raw
  audio or video samples into a compact bitstream — H.264, H.265, VP9,
  AV1, AAC, Opus, MP3, FLAC.
- A **container** (or "format") is the file structure that wraps one
  or more codec bitstreams together with an index, metadata, and
  synchronization info — MP4, MKV, WebM, MOV, AVI.

An MP4 file with H.264 video and AAC audio, and an MKV file with the
exact same H.264 video and AAC audio, contain *bit-for-bit identical*
compressed streams — only the wrapper differs. That's why remuxing
(changing the container without touching the codec data) is instant and
lossless:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mkv -c copy out.mp4
```

`-c copy` tells FFmpeg to copy every stream's compressed bytes
directly into the new container with no decode/re-encode step, which is
why this runs in a fraction of a second regardless of file length.

## Container compatibility

Not every codec can go in every container — MP4 famously can't hold
Vorbis or VP9 well (support is inconsistent across players), and plain AVI
predates most modern codecs entirely. When in doubt, MKV accepts almost
anything, which makes it the safe choice for archival before you've
decided on a final delivery format.

| Container | Good for | Notable limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MP4 | Delivery, web, mobile playback | Subtitles limited to `mov_text`; VP9/Opus support is inconsistent across players |
| MKV | Archival, anything-goes muxing | Slightly less universal hardware/app support than MP4 |
| WebM | Web video, royalty-free delivery | Video limited to VP8/VP9/AV1, audio to Vorbis/Opus |
| MOV | Apple ecosystem, ProRes intermediates | Overlaps heavily with MP4 (same underlying spec family) |
| AVI | Legacy compatibility only | No modern codec or subtitle support worth relying on |

## FFmpeg's codec names vs. common names

| Common name | FFmpeg encoder | FFmpeg decoder name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H.264 / AVC | `libx264` | `h264` |
| H.265 / HEVC | `libx265` | `hevc` |
| VP9 | `libvpx-vp9` | `vp9` |
| AV1 | `libaom-av1` / `libsvtav1` | `av1` |
| AAC | `aac` (built-in) | `aac` |
| Opus | `libopus` | `opus` |

The **en**coder name (what you pass to `-c:v`/`-c:a` when
producing output) can differ from the **de**coder name FFmpeg reports
when reading a file, because several projects (like x264 and x265) provide
third-party encoder implementations of a spec while decoding is handled by
FFmpeg's own built-in decoders.

## Pixel formats: the other axis of compatibility

Beyond codec and container, the **pixel format** (how color/luminance
samples are stored per pixel) determines whether a file plays everywhere:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p out.mp4
```

`yuv420p` (8-bit, 4:2:0 chroma subsampling) is the safest, most
widely-supported pixel format for H.264 delivery — some encoders default
to a different format (10-bit, 4:2:2, or 4:4:4) depending on the source,
which then fails to play in browsers or older hardware decoders that only
understand 8-bit 4:2:0. If a freshly-encoded file "won't play" on a
device or in a browser but opens fine in VLC, a wrong pixel format is
the first thing to check with `ffprobe`.

```bash
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=pix_fmt -of csv=p=0 in.mp4
```

## Inspecting what's actually in a file

```
ffprobe -hide_banner in.mp4
```

prints each stream with its codec, resolution/sample rate, bitrate, and
duration — always worth running before assuming what's inside a file
someone handed you.

## Reading and writing metadata

Containers also carry metadata (title, creation date, GPS location, track
tags) that's separate from the encoded streams:

```bash
ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags in.mp4         # read
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -metadata title="My video" -metadata:s:a:0 language=eng out.mp4  # write
```

`-metadata` sets container-level tags; `-metadata:s:a:0` targets a
specific stream (here, the first audio stream) — useful for tagging
language on multi-track audio without touching the encoded data at all,
since this runs as a `-c copy` remux.
Core Concepts.Filters & filtergraphs:
Every non-trivial transformation in FFmpeg — scaling, cropping,
overlaying, color correction, generating a waveform — goes through the
filtering system. `-vf` and `-af` are shorthand for the common
case; `-filter_complex` is the full syntax for anything with multiple
inputs or outputs.

## -vf and -af: single input, single output

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "scale=1280:720" out.mp4
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af "volume=1.5" out.mp4
```

Chain multiple filters with commas — they run left to right, each
filter's output feeding the next one's input:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "scale=1280:720,eq=brightness=0.06,unsharp" out.mp4
```

## -filter\_complex: multiple inputs/outputs

As soon as a filter needs more than one input stream (like overlaying a
logo onto video) or you need to reuse one stream in two places, you need
labeled pads and the full filtergraph syntax:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i logo.png -filter_complex \
  "[0:v][1:v]overlay=10:10[out]" \
  -map "[out]" -map 0:a out.mp4
```

`[0:v]` and `[1:v]` are input labels (stream `v`ideo from
input `0` and `1`); `[out]` is a custom output label you then
select with `-map`. Anything not explicitly mapped after using
`-filter_complex` is dropped, which is why `-map 0:a` is needed
here to keep the original audio — filtergraphs don't carry audio
through automatically.

## Splitting a stream for multiple uses

```
# produce both a 1080p and a 480p output from one input in one pass
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex \
  "[0:v]split=2[v1][v2]; [v1]scale=1920:1080[v1out]; [v2]scale=854:480[v2out]" \
  -map "[v1out]" -c:v libx264 1080p.mp4 \
  -map "[v2out]" -c:v libx264 480p.mp4
```

`split` duplicates a stream into N identically-labeled copies so
each can be processed independently — useful for generating multiple
renditions (as ABR streaming setups need) without decoding the source
twice.

## A few filters worth knowing

| Filter | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `scale=W:H` | Resize |
| `crop=W:H:X:Y` | Crop to a rectangle |
| `fps=N` | Change/limit frame rate |
| `eq=brightness=:contrast=:saturation=` | Basic color correction |
| `drawtext=text='...'` | Burn text onto frames |
| `overlay=X:Y` | Composite one video/image onto another |
| `concat=n=N:v=1:a=1` | Concatenate streams inside one filtergraph (vs. the concat demuxer) |
| `loudnorm` | EBU R128 loudness normalization |
| `hqdn3d` / `nlmeans` | Denoise (fast/blurry vs. slow/sharper) |
| `yadif` / `bwdif` | Deinterlace (bwdif generally looks better, costs more CPU) |
| `pad=W:H:X:Y` | Add letterbox/pillarbox padding around a smaller frame |
| `setpts=PTS*N` | Speed up/slow down video by rescaling timestamps |
| `atempo=N` | Speed up/slow down audio while preserving pitch (0.5–2.0 per filter instance) |

## Denoising and deinterlacing

Old capture cards, low-light footage, and interlaced broadcast sources
need cleanup before they scale or encode well:

```bash
# denoise (hqdn3d is fast; good default for grainy/noisy footage)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "hqdn3d=4:3:6:4.5" -c:v libx264 -crf 20 out.mp4

# deinterlace (bwdif is the modern default; yadif is the older, faster option)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "bwdif" -c:v libx264 -crf 20 out.mp4
```

Interlaced source footage (common from older TV/broadcast equipment)
shows horizontal "combing" artifacts on motion if it isn't deinterlaced
before scaling or delivery to a progressive-scan display — `ffprobe`
reports the field order (`tt`/`bb` vs `progressive`) if you're unsure
whether a file needs this step.

## Changing speed without changing pitch

```bash
# 2x speed, video and audio together
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]setpts=0.5*PTS[v];[0:a]atempo=2.0[a]" \
  -map "[v]" -map "[a]" out.mp4
```

`setpts` rescales video timestamps (no resampling involved, since video
frames don't need pitch correction); `atempo` time-stretches audio while
keeping pitch natural. Chain multiple `atempo` filters for factors outside
0.5–2.0 (e.g. `atempo=2.0,atempo=2.0` for 4x).

## Building a video from an image sequence

```bash
# numbered frames -> video
ffmpeg -framerate 24 -i frame_%04d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p out.mp4
```

This is the inverse of frame extraction (see
[Common Operations](/ffmpeg/common-operations/)) and is how
render-farm output, screenshot bursts, or stop-motion photo sequences
typically get turned into a deliverable video file.

## Discovering available filters

```bash
ffmpeg -filters              # list every filter this build supports
ffmpeg -h filter=overlay     # show detailed options and defaults for one filter
```

Common Tasks.Common Operations:
The everyday operations you'll reach for most: changing formats, cutting
clips, pulling out audio, and resizing video.

## Converting formats (transcoding)

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mov out.mp4                          # container + default codecs
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac out.mp4     # explicit codecs
ffmpeg -i in.mkv -c copy out.mp4                   # remux only, no re-encode (fast)
```

`-c copy` is much faster and lossless since it just repackages the
existing streams — use it whenever you only need to change the container,
not the codec.

## Trimming / cutting a clip

```
# fast, keyframe-aligned (may be slightly off from the exact timestamp)
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:10 -i in.mp4 -t 5 -c copy clip.mp4

# frame-accurate, re-encodes (slower, exact)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -ss 00:00:10 -t 5 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac clip.mp4
```

`-ss` is the start time, `-t` is the duration to keep; use `-to` instead of
`-t` to specify an absolute end timestamp rather than a duration.

## Extracting audio

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -c:a copy audio.m4a     # copy the existing audio stream as-is
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -c:a libmp3lame -q:a 2 audio.mp3  # re-encode to MP3
```

`-vn` means "no video stream" in the output.

## Scaling / resizing video

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720 out.mp4       # exact size
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:-1 out.mp4        # fixed width, auto height (even)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=-1:720 out.mp4         # fixed height, auto width
```

Use `-2` instead of `-1` for the auto dimension if the target codec
requires even numbers (most H.264 encoders do).

## Changing quality / bitrate

```
# constant quality (recommended for most cases); lower = better, 18-28 is typical
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 out.mp4

# explicit target bitrate instead
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 2M out.mp4

# audio bitrate
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:a aac -b:a 192k out.mp4
```

## Creating a GIF

```
# quick and simple
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=480:-1" out.gif

# higher quality, two-pass palette approach
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "fps=15,scale=480:-1,palettegen" palette.png
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i palette.png \
  -filter_complex "fps=15,scale=480:-1[x];[x][1:v]paletteuse" out.gif
```

## Extracting frames as images

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf fps=1 frame_%04d.png       # one frame per second
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:05 -i in.mp4 -frames:v 1 shot.png  # a single frame at 5s
```

## Generating a thumbnail contact sheet

```bash
# a 4x3 grid of evenly-spaced frames from the whole video
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "select='not(mod(n\,300))',scale=320:-1,tile=4x3" -frames:v 1 sheet.png
```

`select` picks one frame every 300 (roughly every 10s at 30fps); `tile`
arranges the selected frames into a grid image in one pass, which is
handy for quickly previewing a long file without scrubbing through it.

## Concatenating clips

```
# files.txt contains lines like: file 'clip1.mp4'
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i files.txt -c copy joined.mp4
```

The concat demuxer only works cleanly with `-c copy` when every input
shares the same codec/resolution; otherwise re-encode with the
`concat` filter instead.

## Compressing a large video

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 28 -preset slow \
  -c:a aac -b:a 128k out.mp4
```

`-preset` trades encoding speed for compression efficiency (`ultrafast` …
`slower`) — it does not directly affect quality, `-crf` does.

## Overlaying an image or watermark

```
# place logo.png in the bottom-right corner, 10px padding
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i logo.png -filter_complex \
  "overlay=W-w-10:H-h-10" out.mp4
```

`W`/`H` refer to the main video's dimensions and `w`/`h` to
the overlay's, evaluated automatically by the filter — see
[Filters & filtergraphs](/ffmpeg/filters/) for the general syntax.

## Rotating and flipping video

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf transpose=1 out.mp4    # 90° clockwise
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf transpose=2 out.mp4    # 90° counter-clockwise
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf hflip out.mp4          # horizontal mirror
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf vflip out.mp4          # vertical mirror
```

## Fixing audio/video sync drift

```bash
# shift audio 300ms later relative to video
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -itsoffset 0.3 -i in.mp4 -map 0:v -map 1:a -c copy out.mp4

# resample audio to correct gradual drift over a long recording
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v copy -af "aresample=async=1000" out.mp4
```

The first form re-reads the same file twice with different timing offsets
applied to each "copy," taking video from one and audio from the other —
useful for a fixed, constant offset. The second form (`aresample=async`)
nudges the audio clock gradually to correct drift that accumulates over a
long capture, which a fixed offset can't fix since the error isn't
constant.
Common Tasks.Video Encoding:
Encoding is where most of FFmpeg's tunable complexity lives. This page
goes deeper than [Common Operations](/ffmpeg/common-operations/)'
quick bitrate example into the actual decisions worth understanding.

## CRF: constant quality, not constant bitrate

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 -preset medium out.mp4
```

**CRF** (Constant Rate Factor) targets a consistent *perceptual
quality* throughout the video, letting the bitrate float up during
complex/high-motion scenes and down during static ones. This is almost
always what you want for offline encoding (as opposed to streaming, where a
predictable bitrate matters more — see
[Streaming](/ffmpeg/streaming/)).

| Codec | Typical CRF range | Visually lossless around |
| --- | --- | --- |
| libx264 (H.264) | 18–28 | ~18 |
| libx265 (H.265) | 20–30 | ~20 (HEVC's scale isn't 1:1 with x264's) |
| libaom-av1 / libsvtav1 | 25–40 (different scale again) | ~28–30 |

Lower is higher quality and larger file size; there's no universal
"good" number since it depends on content and codec — test a few values
on a representative clip rather than trusting a single rule of thumb.

## Presets: speed vs. compression efficiency

```
ultrafast, superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium, slow, slower, veryslow
```

A slower preset spends more CPU time finding better motion vectors and
mode decisions, producing a *smaller file at the same CRF* — it does
not, by itself, change visual quality at a given CRF the way CRF itself
does. For final delivery encodes, `slow` or `slower` is usually
worth the extra time; for quick previews, `veryfast`.

## Two-pass encoding for a target file size

When you need to hit a specific file size (fitting a video into an email
attachment limit, a Discord upload cap, etc.) rather than a specific
quality, calculate the target bitrate and use two-pass encoding:

```
# target: 8 minutes (480s) into 25MB → ~427kbps total, minus ~128kbps audio → ~300kbps video
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 300k -pass 1 -an -f null /dev/null
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -b:v 300k -pass 2 -c:a aac -b:a 128k out.mp4
```

Pass 1 analyzes the whole file and writes stats (discarding actual
output, hence `-f null /dev/null`); pass 2 uses those stats to
distribute the fixed bitrate budget intelligently across scenes, instead of
applying it uniformly the way single-pass `-b:v` would.

## Resolution and frame rate

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:720 -r 30 out.mp4
```

Downscaling and reducing frame rate both directly reduce bitrate needs
at a given CRF — often a bigger lever than chasing a lower CRF value,
especially for source footage shot at a higher resolution/frame rate than
the delivery target actually needs.

## x264/x265 tuning options

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 20 -tune film out.mp4
```

`-tune` biases the encoder's internal decisions toward a known content
type, which can help more than fiddling with CRF alone:

| Tune | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| `film` | Live-action video with grain |
| `animation` | Cartoons/anime — cel-shaded flat color regions |
| `grain` | Preserves heavy film grain rather than smoothing it away |
| `stillimage` | Slideshows, mostly-static content |
| `fastdecode` | Prioritizes a decoder-friendly stream, useful for low-power playback devices |
| `zerolatency` | Real-time/streaming — disables lookahead buffering (see [Streaming](/ffmpeg/streaming/)) |

## Color space and HDR (avoiding "washed out" output)

Re-encoding HDR or wide-gamut source footage without preserving its color
metadata is a common cause of output looking washed out, oversaturated, or
just wrong on some players — the pixel data is fine, but the container
no longer tells the player how to interpret it:

```bash
# copy color metadata through explicitly rather than letting it default
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx265 -crf 20 \
  -color_primaries bt2020 -color_trc smpte2084 -colorspace bt2020nc \
  out.mp4
```

Check what the source actually uses before guessing:

```bash
ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \
  -show_entries stream=color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space \
  -of default=nw=1 in.mp4
```

Standard-dynamic-range (SDR) footage almost always uses `bt709`; HDR10
content uses `bt2020` primaries with the `smpte2084` (PQ) transfer
function. Converting HDR to SDR (tone mapping) is a separate, lossy step
best done with the `zscale` or `tonemap` filters rather than just
dropping the metadata, which leaves the pixel values HDR-encoded but
mislabels them as SDR.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-crf N` | Constant-quality target (lower = better) |
| `-preset <name>` | Encoding speed vs. compression tradeoff |
| `-tune <name>` | Bias encoder decisions toward a known content type |
| `-b:v <rate>` | Target average video bitrate |
| `-maxrate` / `-bufsize` | Cap peak bitrate (needed for streaming targets) |
| `-pass 1` / `-pass 2` | Two-pass encoding for accurate target size |
| `-pix_fmt yuv420p` | Force a widely-compatible pixel format (needed for some players) |
| `-color_primaries` / `-color_trc` / `-colorspace` | Explicitly set/preserve color metadata |
Common Tasks.Audio Processing:
Audio is cheaper to encode than video but has its own set of decisions
— codec choice, quality control, loudness, and combining multiple
tracks.

## Choosing a codec

| Codec | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| AAC | Default choice for MP4/streaming; near-universal playback support |
| Opus | Best quality per bit at low-to-mid bitrates; ideal for voice, WebM, calls |
| MP3 | Maximum legacy compatibility; slightly less efficient than AAC/Opus |
| FLAC | Lossless archival; large files, exact reproduction |

## Constant bitrate vs. variable quality

```
# constant bitrate: predictable size, fine for streaming
ffmpeg -i in.wav -c:a aac -b:a 192k out.m4a

# variable quality (VBR): better quality-per-byte, size varies with content
ffmpeg -i in.wav -c:a libmp3lame -q:a 2 out.mp3      # LAME scale: 0 (best) - 9 (worst)
ffmpeg -i in.wav -c:a aac -q:a 2 out.m4a             # native AAC VBR, roughly 1(worst)-5(best)
ffmpeg -i in.wav -c:a libopus -b:a 96k out.opus      # Opus is always effectively VBR internally
```

## Loudness normalization

Files from different sources often have wildly different perceived
loudness. `loudnorm` implements the EBU R128 standard used by
broadcasters:

```
# single pass (fast, less accurate)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5:LRA=11 out.mp4

# two-pass (measure, then apply precisely) — recommended for anything final
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -af loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5:LRA=11:print_format=json -f null -
# read the printed measured_* values, then re-run with:
# loudnorm=I=-16:TP=-1.5:LRA=11:measured_I=...:measured_TP=...:measured_LRA=...:measured_thresh=...:linear=true
```

`-16` LUFS is a common streaming-platform target (Spotify, YouTube
are close to this); podcasts commonly target `-16` to `-19`.

## Detecting and removing silence

```bash
# detect: prints start/end timestamps of silent sections to stderr
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af silencedetect=noise=-30dB:d=0.5 -f null -

# remove: strips silence from start/end and long silences from the middle
ffmpeg -i in.wav -af silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-30dB:stop_periods=-1:stop_threshold=-30dB out.wav
```

`silencedetect` is non-destructive and just reports where silence occurs
(useful for scripting cut points); `silenceremove` actually trims it.
`noise`/`threshold` is the volume floor considered "silent"; tune it a
few dB up or down depending on the recording's noise floor.

## Mixing multiple audio tracks

```
# mix voice.mp3 and music.mp3 into one output, music quieter
ffmpeg -i voice.mp3 -i music.mp3 -filter_complex \
  "[1:a]volume=0.3[bg];[0:a][bg]amix=inputs=2:duration=first[out]" \
  -map "[out]" mixed.mp3
```

`amix` sums multiple audio streams into one; `duration=first`
trims the mix to the length of the first input rather than the longest
(the default), which matters when the background track is longer than the
voiceover.

## Extracting and replacing audio

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vn -c:a copy audio.m4a               # extract as-is
ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -i new-audio.wav -c:v copy \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 -shortest out.mp4               # replace audio track entirely
```

`-shortest` stops the output at the length of the shorter of the two
inputs, avoiding a trailing silent/frozen tail if the new audio and
original video aren't exactly the same length.

## Working with multiple audio tracks/languages

```bash
ffprobe -v error -select_streams a -show_entries stream=index:stream_tags=language in.mkv
ffmpeg -i in.mkv -map 0:v -map 0:a:0 -map 0:a:1 -c copy out.mkv   # keep two specific audio tracks
```

`-map` with an explicit stream index is how you selectively keep, drop,
or reorder tracks in a multi-language file rather than accepting
FFmpeg's default of "one video, one audio, no subtitles."

Streaming & Live.Streaming & Live Input:
Beyond converting files, FFmpeg reads directly from cameras, screens, and
microphones, and can push a live encode out to streaming platforms.

## Capturing a webcam (Linux)

```bash
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -list_formats all -i /dev/video0   # see what the device supports
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -framerate 30 -video_size 1280x720 \
  -i /dev/video0 -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast out.mp4
```

## Capturing the screen (Linux/X11)

```
# full screen, from display :0
ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 30 -video_size 1920x1080 -i :0.0 out.mp4

# a specific region, offset from the top-left
ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 30 -video_size 800x600 -i :0.0+100,200 out.mp4

# capture screen + microphone together
ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 30 -i :0.0 -f pulse -i default \
  -c:v libx264 -c:a aac out.mp4
```

Wayland compositors don't support `x11grab` directly; use
`-f pipewire` (where supported) or a compositor-provided portal-based
capture tool that hands FFmpeg a file descriptor instead. On Arch running
a Wayland session (GNOME, KDE, Sway), check whether your compositor
exposes a portal-based screencast before reaching for X11-only tools.

## Streaming to RTMP (Twitch, YouTube, etc.)

```bash
ffmpeg -f x11grab -framerate 30 -i :0.0 -f pulse -i default \
  -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -b:v 4500k -maxrate 4500k -bufsize 9000k \
  -c:a aac -b:a 160k -f flv \
  "rtmp://live.twitch.tv/app/<your-stream-key>"
```

Streaming needs a **capped** bitrate (`-maxrate` +
`-bufsize`), unlike offline CRF encoding, because the platform expects
a roughly steady rate it can forward in real time — a CRF encode's
bitrate spikes during complex scenes would overflow the upload pipe.

## Automatically reconnecting a flaky stream

```bash
ffmpeg -reconnect 1 -reconnect_streamed 1 -reconnect_delay_max 5 \
  -i "rtmp://source.example.com/live/stream" -c copy out.mp4
```

These `-reconnect*` flags apply to the *input* side and matter most
when ingesting from an unreliable network source (a remote camera, an
upstream restream) rather than when pushing your own local encode out —
without them, a dropped connection kills the whole ffmpeg process instead
of retrying.

## Generating an HLS stream

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac \
  -f hls -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_filename "seg_%03d.ts" playlist.m3u8
```

This splits the output into 6-second `.ts` segments plus an
`.m3u8` playlist referencing them — the format most video players
and CDNs expect for adaptive streaming. `hls_playlist_type vod` marks
it as a complete, seekable video-on-demand stream rather than an
open-ended live one.

## Multi-bitrate HLS (adaptive streaming)

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex \
  "[0:v]split=3[v1][v2][v3]; \
   [v1]scale=1920:1080[v1out]; [v2]scale=1280:720[v2out]; [v3]scale=854:480[v3out]" \
  -map "[v1out]" -c:v:0 libx264 -b:v:0 5000k \
  -map "[v2out]" -c:v:1 libx264 -b:v:1 2800k \
  -map "[v3out]" -c:v:2 libx264 -b:v:2 1400k \
  -map a:0 -map a:0 -map a:0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k \
  -f hls -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0 v:1,a:1 v:2,a:2" \
  -hls_segment_filename "stream_%v/data%03d.ts" \
  -master_pl_name master.m3u8 stream_%v/playlist.m3u8
```

This produces three renditions from one source in a single pass (via
`split`, as covered in
[Filters & filtergraphs](/ffmpeg/filters/#splitting-a-stream-for-multiple-uses))
plus a master playlist a player can switch between based on the viewer's
bandwidth — the same idea behind YouTube's or Netflix's quality selector.

## Reducing latency

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-tune zerolatency` | x264 preset tuned for real-time, low-buffer encoding |
| `-g N` | Set keyframe interval explicitly (shorter = more seekable, more overhead) |
| `-fflags nobuffer` | Reduce input buffering when reading a live source |
| `-flags low_delay` | Ask the decoder to minimize its own internal buffering |

Advanced.Hardware Acceleration:
Software encoding (libx264, libx265) uses the CPU and gives the best
quality-per-bit, but is slow relative to real time on demanding sources.
Dedicated encoding hardware built into most modern GPUs trades some
efficiency for dramatically higher throughput.

## Which API for which hardware

| Vendor | API | Encoder names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA | NVENC | `h264_nvenc`, `hevc_nvenc`, `av1_nvenc` (RTX 40-series+) |
| Intel | Quick Sync (QSV) | `h264_qsv`, `hevc_qsv`, `av1_qsv` |
| AMD / Intel (Linux) | VAAPI | `h264_vaapi`, `hevc_vaapi` |
| Apple Silicon / Intel Macs | VideoToolbox | `h264_videotoolbox`, `hevc_videotoolbox` |

## NVIDIA (NVENC)

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v h264_nvenc -preset p5 -cq 23 out.mp4
```

NVENC uses its own preset names (`p1` fastest … `p7` slowest/
best) and `-cq` instead of `-crf` for quality-based encoding. Add
`-hwaccel cuda` before `-i` to decode on the GPU too, avoiding a
CPU round-trip entirely for transcodes:

```bash
ffmpeg -hwaccel cuda -i in.mp4 -c:v h264_nvenc -cq 23 out.mp4
```

## VAAPI (Linux, Intel/AMD)

```bash
ffmpeg -vaapi_device /dev/dri/renderD128 \
  -hwaccel vaapi -hwaccel_output_format vaapi -i in.mp4 \
  -vf 'format=nv12,hwupload' -c:v h264_vaapi out.mp4
```

VAAPI needs explicit format conversion/upload steps in the filtergraph
(`format=nv12,hwupload`) because frames must physically move into
GPU-accessible memory before the hardware encoder can touch them —
this is the step people most often forget, producing a cryptic error about
an unsupported pixel format.

Find your render device with:

```bash
ls /dev/dri/
vainfo   # (from the libva-utils package) lists supported profiles/entrypoints
```

On Arch, `vainfo` is packaged as `libva-utils`
(`sudo pacman -S libva-utils`), and you'll also want the vendor-specific
driver package — `intel-media-driver` (newer Intel iGPUs) or
`libva-mesa-driver` (AMD, and older Intel) — installed before VAAPI
will report any usable profiles.

## Intel Quick Sync (QSV)

```bash
ffmpeg -hwaccel qsv -i in.mp4 -c:v h264_qsv -global_quality 23 out.mp4
```

## Hardware decode only (software encode)

Hardware acceleration isn't all-or-nothing — decoding on the GPU while
still encoding on the CPU is a common middle ground when you want
libx264's quality-per-bit but the source is heavy enough that decode
alone is a bottleneck:

```bash
ffmpeg -hwaccel cuda -hwaccel_output_format cuda -i in.mp4 \
  -vf "hwdownload,format=nv12" -c:v libx264 -crf 20 out.mp4
```

`hwdownload` pulls decoded frames back from GPU memory into normal system
memory before handing them to a software encoder, which expects frames
it can access directly — skipping it is a common source of "impossible
to convert" filter errors when mixing hardware decode with software
filters or encoders.

## Quality tradeoffs

At the same file size, hardware encoders generally produce visibly worse
quality than `libx264`/`libx265` at a comparable CRF — the
efficiency gap has narrowed on recent hardware (especially NVENC on RTX
40-series+) but hasn't closed. Use hardware encoding when speed matters
more than squeezing out every last bit of efficiency: live streaming, bulk
transcoding jobs, or real-time preview generation.

## Checking what your build/hardware supports

```bash
ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders | grep -E "nvenc|vaapi|qsv|videotoolbox"
ffmpeg -hide_banner -hwaccels           # list hwaccel APIs this build was compiled with
```

If a hardware path isn't available (no compatible GPU, missing driver, or
a headless/CI environment), the pragmatic approach for a script or app is
to attempt the hardware encoder first, catch a non-zero exit code, and
fall back to a software encoder rather than requiring the caller to know
in advance what hardware is present.
Advanced.Subtitles:
FFmpeg handles subtitles two fundamentally different ways: as a
**separate muxed track** a player can toggle on/off, or
**burned in** (permanently rendered into the video pixels). The
right choice depends entirely on whether the viewer needs to be able to
turn them off.

## Muxing subtitles as a toggleable track

```
# MP4 (needs mov_text, MP4's native subtitle codec)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -i subs.srt -c:v copy -c:a copy -c:s mov_text out.mp4

# MKV (accepts SRT/ASS as-is, no conversion needed)
ffmpeg -i in.mkv -i subs.srt -c copy -c:s srt out.mkv
```

MP4 can only hold the limited `mov_text` subtitle format (no
styling), which is why `.ass` subtitles with custom fonts/positioning
are usually delivered in MKV instead.

## Burning subtitles in (hard subs)

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subs.srt" -c:a copy out.mp4

# ASS subtitles keep their styling (fonts, colors, positioning) when burned in
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subs.ass" -c:a copy out.mp4
```

Burning in requires a full video re-encode (subtitles become part of the
pixels, so `-c:v copy` isn't possible) and, unlike a muxed track, can
never be turned off by the viewer — useful for social media clips
where autoplay is usually muted and captions need to always be visible.

## Font lookup on Linux (a common `subtitles=` gotcha)

The `subtitles` filter renders through `libass`, which relies on
`fontconfig` to find fonts referenced by name in an `.ass` file's style
definitions. On a minimal Arch install (or a Docker image built from one),
missing fonts silently fall back to a generic default rather than erroring,
which is confusing when styling "doesn't seem to apply":

```bash
# make sure fontconfig and a reasonable font set are present
sudo pacman -S fontconfig noto-fonts

# point libass at a specific font directory if the referenced font isn't system-installed
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf "subtitles=subs.ass:fontsdir=/path/to/fonts" -c:a copy out.mp4
```

## Extracting subtitles from a file

```
ffprobe -i in.mkv                          # find the subtitle stream index first
ffmpeg -i in.mkv -map 0:s:0 out.srt        # extract the first subtitle stream
```

## Converting between subtitle formats

```bash
ffmpeg -i subs.srt subs.vtt     # SRT → WebVTT, for HTML5 <track>
ffmpeg -i subs.ass subs.srt     # ASS → SRT (styling is lost — SRT can't express it)
```

## Quick reference

| Format | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| SRT | Plain text, timestamps only, near-universal support |
| ASS/SSA | Rich styling, positioning, fonts — common for anime/fansubs |
| WebVTT | SRT-like, the web standard for HTML5 `<track>` |
| mov\_text | MP4's limited native subtitle codec, no styling |
Advanced.Scripting & Automation:
Running FFmpeg by hand doesn't scale past a handful of files. This page
covers shell-level batch processing, machine-readable progress, and
reliable failure detection.

## Batch processing in the shell

```
# re-encode every mp4 in a directory to a smaller CRF
for f in *.mp4; do
  ffmpeg -i "$f" -c:v libx264 -crf 28 -c:a copy "compressed_$f"
done

# parallel version using GNU parallel (much faster on multi-core machines)
ls *.mp4 | parallel -j4 ffmpeg -i {} -c:v libx264 -crf 28 -c:a copy compressed_{}
```

Encoding is CPU-bound and each file is independent, so running several
in parallel (bounded to roughly your core count) is usually the single
biggest speedup available for a batch job, more impactful than tuning any
individual encode's preset. On Arch, `parallel` is packaged separately:
`sudo pacman -S parallel`.

## Machine-readable progress

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -progress pipe:1 -nostats out.mp4
```

Instead of the default human-readable stderr status line, this streams
`key=value` pairs (`frame=`, `fps=`, `out_time_ms=`,
`progress=continue`/`end`) to stdout — straightforward for a
wrapper script or GUI to parse into a progress bar, since you can compute a
percentage from `out_time_ms` against the known input duration.

## Detecting failures reliably

FFmpeg exits non-zero on failure, but stderr is verbose even on success
(codec banners, stream info), so don't treat any stderr output as an
error — check the exit code instead:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 out.mp4 2>ffmpeg.log
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Encoding failed, see ffmpeg.log"
  exit 1
fi
```

## A minimal CI-friendly wrapper

For scheduled jobs or CI pipelines, three flags remove the most common
sources of a script hanging or silently misbehaving unattended:

```bash
ffmpeg -y -hide_banner -loglevel error -nostdin -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 out.mp4
```

`-y` avoids the interactive overwrite prompt (which hangs forever with no
terminal attached); `-nostdin` disables ffmpeg's interactive keyboard
controls entirely, which otherwise can misinterpret unrelated stdin
input (common when a process's stdin is connected to a pipe in CI) as a
command like pause or quit.

## Validating output before treating a job as done

An exit code of 0 means ffmpeg didn't error, but a quick sanity check on
the actual output catches the rarer case of a technically-successful run
that produced something unusable (e.g. zero-duration or zero-stream
output from a malformed input):

```bash
ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 out.mp4
```

An empty result or `N/A` here is worth treating as a failure even though
`ffmpeg`'s own exit code was 0.

Reference.Troubleshooting:
A lookup table for the error messages and symptoms people actually hit,
organized by what FFmpeg prints rather than by topic. If you're
scripting FFmpeg calls (see [Scripting & Automation](/ffmpeg/scripting-automation/)),
most of these are worth pattern-matching on stderr to give a caller a
clearer error than "ffmpeg exited 1."

## `Unknown encoder 'libx265'` (or similar)

Your build wasn't compiled with that encoder. Check what's actually
available:

```bash
ffmpeg -encoders | grep -i x265
```

On Arch, the official repo package is a full build with essentially
everything enabled — see
[Build flavors & codec support](/ffmpeg/getting-started/) — so this
usually means either a different, more minimal FFmpeg build is on `PATH`
(check `which ffmpeg` and `ffmpeg -version`), or a typo in the encoder
name (`libx265` not `x265`, `libx264` not `x264`).

## `Could not find tag for codec ... in stream ... codec not currently supported in container`

The target container can't hold that codec — for example, trying to mux
VP9 into a plain `.avi`, or Opus into `.mp4` on an older FFmpeg build.
Either switch containers (MKV accepts almost anything, per
[Containers & Codecs](/ffmpeg/containers-codecs/)) or re-encode to a
codec the container supports, rather than trying to force a `-c copy`
remux.

## `Error while opening encoder... maybe incorrect parameters such as bit_rate, rate, width or height`

Usually a dimension that isn't valid for the chosen encoder — most H.264/
H.265 encoders require even width and height. If you scaled with a single
fixed dimension and `-1` for the other, switch to `-2`:

```bash
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -vf scale=1280:-2 -c:v libx264 out.mp4
```

`-2` rounds the auto-computed dimension to the nearest even number;
`-1` doesn't, which is fine for some codecs/filters but fails for
libx264/libx265's macroblock-based encoding.

## `Unsupported pixel format` (often from a VAAPI/hardware filter chain)

A hardware encoder or `hwupload`-based filter was handed frames in a
format it doesn't accept directly. See the hardware-decode/encode format
conversion steps in [Hardware Acceleration](/ffmpeg/hardware-acceleration/)
— you almost always need an explicit `format=nv12,hwupload` (VAAPI) or
`hwdownload,format=nv12` (mixing hardware decode with software encode)
somewhere in the filter chain.

## Output has no audio

Check for an accidental `-an` in the command, and confirm the container
actually supports the audio codec you asked for:

```bash
ffprobe out.mp4 -show_streams -select_streams a
```

An empty result means no audio stream made it into the output at all —
work backward from there: was `-map` used and did it exclude the audio
input, or did the container reject the codec silently in an older build?

## `moov atom not found` / file won't open, especially after a crash or kill

MP4 by default writes its index (the `moov` atom) at the *end* of the
file, once encoding finishes — if the process is killed (`SIGKILL`,
power loss, a crash) before that final write, the file is left without a
valid index and most players refuse to open it. Two ways to avoid this
going forward:

```bash
# write the moov atom at the start instead (slightly slower, safe to interrupt)
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -movflags +faststart out.mp4

# or, for progressively-written recordings, use fragmented MP4
ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c:v libx264 -movflags frag_keyframe+empty_moov out.mp4
```

`+faststart` also has an unrelated, commonly-cited benefit: it lets web
players start playback before the whole file downloads, since the index
is available immediately at the front of the file.

## `Non-monotonic DTS` / `Application provided invalid, non monotonically increasing dts`

The input's timestamps are out of order or discontinuous — common with
screen recordings, concatenated streams, or files from buggy encoders.
A safe general fix when you don't need exact original timestamps:

```bash
ffmpeg -fflags +genpts -i in.mp4 -c copy out.mp4
```

`+genpts` regenerates presentation timestamps from scratch rather than
trusting the (broken) ones in the source.

## The process hangs forever with no output

Almost always one of:

- An interactive prompt is waiting on stdin (overwrite confirmation) with
  nothing connected to answer it — add `-y` and `-nostdin`, as covered in
  [Scripting & Automation](/ffmpeg/scripting-automation/#a-minimal-ci-friendly-wrapper).
- A stderr (or stdout, if using `-progress pipe:1`) pipe buffer filled up
  because the calling code isn't reading it. Whatever language is driving
  the process, make sure both stdout and stderr are actively drained
  concurrently rather than read sequentially after the process exits —
  ffmpeg can block indefinitely writing to a full pipe while the caller is
  blocked waiting for it to finish.
- A live input (webcam, RTMP source, screen capture) that FFmpeg is
  correctly waiting on — check whether the command was actually meant to
  read from a file instead of a device/network source.

## General debugging approach

```bash
ffmpeg -v verbose -i in.mp4 ... out.mp4 2>debug.log
```

Raising `-loglevel`/`-v` to `verbose` or `debug` (rather than the
default `info`) surfaces the specific reason a filter, muxer, or codec
rejected something, which the default log level often summarizes too
tersely to act on. Combine with `ffprobe` on both the input and any
partial output to confirm what FFmpeg is actually seeing at each stage,
rather than guessing from the command alone.
Reference.FAQ:
## Why does `-ss` behave differently depending on where I put it?

Placing `-ss` *before* `-i` tells the demuxer to seek directly to the
nearest keyframe at or before that timestamp, which is fast but can be up
to a couple of seconds off. Placing it *after* `-i` decodes from the very
start and discards frames until the exact timestamp, which is precise but
much slower on long files. For most trimming, seek-before-input plus a
small re-encode at the cut point gives a good speed/accuracy balance.

## Should I use `-crf` or `-b:v`?

Use `-crf` (constant quality) for most cases — you tell the encoder how
much quality loss is acceptable and file size follows naturally, which
generally looks better per byte than a fixed bitrate. Use an explicit
`-b:v` target bitrate only when you have a hard size or bandwidth
constraint to hit, such as fitting a file under a strict upload limit or
matching a fixed streaming bitrate.

## Why did `-c copy` fail or produce a broken file?

`-c copy` repackages existing streams without touching their encoding,
so it only works when the target container actually supports those
codecs — for example, some containers don't support certain subtitle or
audio codec combinations. If a "copy" remux fails or plays back oddly,
drop `-c copy` and let FFmpeg re-encode with the output container's
default codecs instead.

## Why does my output look blocky or low-quality?

Almost always the CRF value is too high (too much compression) or an
explicit bitrate is too low for the resolution and motion in the source.
Lower the `-crf` value (e.g. from 28 to 20) or raise `-b:v`, and consider
a slower `-preset`, which spends more encoding time finding better
compression at the same quality target.

## Does FFmpeg support hardware-accelerated encoding?

Yes, if your build was compiled with support for it and your GPU/driver
provides it: NVENC (NVIDIA), QSV (Intel Quick Sync), VAAPI (Linux/Intel/AMD),
and VideoToolbox (macOS) are common options, selected via codec names like
`-c:v h264_nvenc` or `-c:v h264_vaapi` in place of the software encoder.
Hardware encoding is much faster but generally produces slightly larger
files than a software encoder at the same visual quality.

## How do I avoid quality loss when editing a video multiple times?

Every re-encode of a lossy codec (H.264, H.265, most audio codecs) loses
some quality, so repeated edit-and-export cycles compound that loss.
Where possible, do `-c copy` operations (trimming at keyframes,
remuxing) that don't touch the encoded data, or work from a lossless or
high-bitrate intermediate and only export the lossy final version once,
at the end of your edit chain.

## Why won't my file play in a browser or on a phone, even though VLC opens it fine?

VLC's decoders are far more permissive than a browser's or a phone's
hardware decoder. The usual culprits are a non-standard pixel format
(10-bit or 4:2:2/4:4:4 instead of 8-bit 4:2:0), an MP4 whose index
(`moov` atom) is at the end of the file, or a codec profile/level higher
than the target device supports. See
[Pixel formats](/ffmpeg/containers-codecs/#pixel-formats-the-other-axis-of-compatibility)
and the `moov atom` entry in [Troubleshooting](/ffmpeg/troubleshooting/)
for the specific fixes.

## A few more common questions

**Why does my output have no audio?**
Check that you didn't accidentally include `-an`, and that the
container supports the audio codec you asked for (e.g. plain AVI can't hold
Opus). Run `ffprobe out.mp4` to confirm which streams actually made
it into the file. See also [Troubleshooting](/ffmpeg/troubleshooting/).

**Why is -filter\_complex needed instead of -vf sometimes?**
`-vf`/`-af` are shorthand for a filtergraph with exactly one
input and one output. As soon as a filter needs multiple inputs (like
`overlay`, which takes the main video and the watermark) or produces
multiple outputs, you need the full `-filter_complex` syntax. See
[Filters & filtergraphs](/ffmpeg/filters/).

**How do I check which hardware encoders my build supports?**
`ffmpeg -encoders 2>/dev/null | grep -E "nvenc|vaapi|qsv|videotoolbox"`
— see [Hardware Acceleration](/ffmpeg/hardware-acceleration/)
for setup per platform.

**Where do I look when a command just errors out with a message I don't recognize?**
[Troubleshooting](/ffmpeg/troubleshooting/) is organized by the actual
error text FFmpeg prints, for exactly this case.
